headline: The dollar's seven-day climb paused on Tuesday as US stocks fell again before Nvidia's results and US yields eased. The euro got back to $1.10, while the Aussie and kiwi slipped further.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: The dollar index ended Tuesday a touch lower, near 103.5, its first down day after seven gains. Firm retail sales kept a December Fed hike all but certain, but a weak factory report and another stock sell-off pulled US yields down.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: High oil from the US–Iran war has kept US inflation at about twice the Federal Reserve's 2% goal, and hot October price figures made a December rate hike all but certain, lifting the dollar to its highest since April 2025. What changed: October retail sales rose 0.2%, a little above forecast, with spending outside cars stronger. Industrial production then fell 0.4% against a forecast rise, though mostly because utilities gave back a weather-driven jump; factory output itself rose. A US homebuilder survey sank to its lowest since 2012, and US stocks fell for a second day before Nvidia's results. The two-year Treasury yield fell about 0.09 point to 4.79%, and the dollar index slipped about 0.1% after touching a new high near 103.7. What it means: The data still say the Fed has no reason to stop, so bets on a quarter-point December hike rose to about 97%, while the chance of a half-point move all but vanished. Lower yields on a scary stock day took a little shine off the dollar. The question: do the Fed's meeting minutes show officials ready to keep hiking into next year?

Wednesday, November 18 at 1:00 PM, minutes of the Fed's October meeting. Thursday, November 19 at 7:30 AM, weekly jobless claims. The Fed decides on December 9.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro dipped below $1.097 after firm US retail sales, a fresh low since April 2025, then climbed back to about $1.10 as US yields fell in the afternoon. It ended Tuesday about flat.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The euro has slid for weeks on weak growth, costly energy and France's debt worries, while bets on faster US rate rises pushed it to its lowest in more than a year and a half. What changed: No euro-area news of note. The morning's US retail figures took the euro to a new low, then a weak US factory report, falling stocks and lower US yields let it recover to about $1.1006 by the New York close. A European Central Bank hike on December 17 is still widely expected. What it means: The euro's moves are still set mostly in Washington. A dip in US yields gives it room to breathe, but as long as the Fed looks set to hike for longer than the European Central Bank, the rate gap keeps working against it. Hedge funds bet against the euro while big long-term investors bet for it, so a surprise either way could bring a sharp move. The question: does President Christine Lagarde sound ready to keep hiking after December?

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: The pound rose about 0.15% to roughly $1.321 on Tuesday as the dollar paused. UK pay growth cooled exactly as forecast, so UK inflation figures early Wednesday, November 18 will decide whether a second December hike stays likely.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, its first hike since 2023, and Governor Andrew Bailey said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts. The pound then slid as US rates rose faster. What changed: Regular pay grew 3.5% from a year earlier, down from 3.7% and in line with forecasts, and unemployment fell to 4.6%. But payrolls dropped and job vacancies hit their lowest since 2021, so the jobs picture was mixed. The pound dipped near $1.317 in the morning, then recovered above $1.32 as US yields fell. Markets still give a second December hike about a seven-in-ten chance. What it means: Pay is cooling, but slowly, which keeps the hike case alive without strengthening it. That puts all the weight on Wednesday's inflation figures. The question: does UK inflation climb to 3.6% as forecast?

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The dollar slipped about 0.1% to roughly 159.4 yen on Tuesday, its third straight dip, after briefly falling below 159. Falling stocks and lower US yields helped the yen, while Japan's warnings keep the dollar below 160.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The yen is weak because Japanese rates are far below others. The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25% and is expected to hike in December, and Japan spent about 15 trillion yen buying its currency after the dollar neared 164 yen in late July. What changed: A second day of falling stocks sent some money into the yen, and the drop in US two-year yields in the afternoon narrowed the gap that has pulled money out of Japan. The dollar dipped under 159 yen at one point and closed near 159.35. Japan's finance minister Satsuki Katayama repeated that the government will respond to sharp currency swings. What it means: The yen still gains when markets get scared, but the wide rate gap keeps pulling it back. The threat of Japan buying yen near 160 remains the main brake. The question: does a deeper stock sell-off after Nvidia's results lift the yen further?

Wednesday, November 18 at 1:00 PM, the Fed's minutes. Any statement from Japan's finance ministry can move the yen at any hour. The Bank of Japan decides on December 18.

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: The dollar ended Tuesday near 0.840 francs, about flat, after setting an 18-month high overnight. Falling stocks and a US strike on an Iranian island brought the franc little extra demand.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The franc is a safe haven that gains when markets get scared, but Swiss inflation is low and the Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero, so it pays nothing to hold. What changed: No Swiss news. The dollar touched about 0.841 francs in Asian trading, its highest since mid-2025, then eased as US yields fell. A US official confirmed a strike on an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island, in answer to drone attacks on Bahrain, but it did not set off a rush to safety. What it means: As long as US rates keep rising, holding francs stays costly, and only a real scare brings buyers back. The yen, not the franc, has been the safe haven of choice this week. The question: does Nvidia's report or the Gulf turn the tech slide into a wider fright?

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Aussie ended Tuesday about 0.3% lower near 67.4 US cents, after touching its lowest since January, as US stocks fell again. Australian wage figures come at 6:30 PM CT Tuesday, November 17, and jobs figures a day later.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks, while unemployment sits at a five-year high. Weak Chinese figures and falling gold have pushed the Aussie lower. What changed: Minutes of the November meeting showed a split board, six to three, and Governor Michele Bullock said inflation risks still lean upward, but Australia's big banks still call 4.85% the peak. A second day of falling US stocks weighed on the Aussie, which tends to track market mood, though it recovered a little as the US dollar paused. What it means: A split board and a softer economy suggest the hikes are near their end, so the Aussie has little support of its own when markets get nervous. Big long-term investors bet heavily against it, so good news could spark a sharp bounce. The question: do this week's wage and jobs figures show enough pressure to keep the bank hiking?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up, all times CT: Tuesday, November 17 at 6:30 PM, Australian wages for the third quarter (forecast 1.0%). Wednesday, November 18 at 6:30 PM, jobs figures for October (unemployment forecast 4.7%). Nvidia's results overnight could also swing the mood. The Reserve Bank of Australia decides on December 8.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The US dollar ended Tuesday about flat near 1.429 Canadian dollars. Canada had no news, and a mixed day for oil, with Brent up and US crude down, left the loonie little changed.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October, but job losses and October inflation of 3.1%, with core prices near the bank's 2% goal, have cut bets on a December hike to a bit under half. What changed: No Canadian news. Brent crude edged up while US crude, the closer guide for Canadian oil, slipped about 1%. The US dollar eased slightly against the loonie as US yields fell, ending near 1.4293. What it means: With the Bank of Canada likely to wait and the Fed likely to hike, the rate gap works against the loonie, and oil is its main cushion. A falling stock market adds a little pressure, since the loonie tends to weaken when investors get nervous. The question: does oil hold steady while the Gulf stays tense?

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: The kiwi fell about 0.4% to roughly 54.9 US cents on Tuesday, staying near its lowest in more than a year and a half. Falling stocks weighed on it, and a flat dairy auction gave it no help.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The kiwi sank as rising unemployment cut bets on a December Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike. The bank held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. What changed: The Global Dairy Trade auction left prices unchanged overall after a 3% rise last time. Milk powder, New Zealand's main dairy export, rose, while butter and cheese fell. Earlier, the bank's survey showed businesses' inflation expectations barely moved, and its stability report warned that global financial risks are rising. A second day of falling US stocks weighed on the kiwi, which tends to track market mood. What it means: Firm milk powder prices still help New Zealand's income, but nothing at home is pushing the bank toward a December hike, so the kiwi lacks support as US rates rise. Hedge funds have sharply added to bets against it, so good news could spark a quick bounce. The question: does Governor Anna Breman hint at a December hike when she speaks Wednesday, November 18?

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Brent crude ended Tuesday about 0.6% higher near $92.9 a barrel after an early dip toward $91.6, while US crude fell about 1%. A US strike on an Iranian missile site kept war risk in view, but the supply-surplus outlook still set the tone.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Oil soared in October on the US–Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, then fell as Gulf exports recovered. Brent settled at $92.44 on Monday after a 3.6% drop as traders bet supply will outrun demand. What changed: Selling ran on overnight, then buyers returned after another tanker was hit in the Gulf and Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired drones at a US base in Bahrain, which says it intercepted them. In the afternoon a US official confirmed American jets hit an Iranian missile site on Qeshm Island in response. Prices barely reacted. What it means: Traders are weighing a supply glut against attacks that keep coming, and so far the glut wins the bigger moves. Pricier oil helps the Canadian dollar and weighs on energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area. The question: does the back-and-forth between the US and Iran start to disrupt flows again?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up, all times CT: Wednesday, November 18, weekly US crude stock figures. OPEC+ meets on November 29 to set output for 2027. Any confirmed Gulf attack can move prices at any hour.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: Gold fell about 0.5% to near $3,847 an ounce on Tuesday, close to Monday's 13-month low. Even falling stocks and lower US yields brought it no lift, as bets on a December Fed hike firmed.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Gold slipped below $4,000 last week after hot US inflation figures and Fed talk of more hikes lifted the dollar and US yields. On Monday it hit its lowest since October 2025, near $3,840. What changed: Firm US retail sales pushed the odds of a December Fed hike up to about 97%. Gold slid with them and stayed down even after US yields fell back and stocks sold off, which would usually help it. What it means: Gold pays no interest, so while the Fed is expected to keep raising rates, holding it gets costlier, and that still outweighs its appeal in wartime or a stock slump. Hedge funds still bet strongly on gold, so a further slide could force some of them out. The question: do the Fed's minutes back more hikes, or does a stock-market scare finally bring buyers back?

calls.text: Brent near $114 after Aramco cleared its Dhahran headquarters: a Houthi hit that cuts Saudi output lifts Brent past its May highs and supports the loonie; a quiet weekend lets it ease toward $110
calls.note: Both happened in turn: Houthi attacks lifted Brent to about $117 on Friday without a confirmed cut to Saudi output, then a quiet weekend and talks in Tehran took it to about $110 by Monday.

calls.text: Canada retail sales Fri 7:30 AM CT (about +1.3% expected for August): a strong rebound lifts bets on Bank of Canada hikes beyond October 28; a miss keeps it to one
calls.note: Sales rose 1.2%, a touch under the 1.3% expected, so neither a strong beat nor a miss; Bank of Canada hike pricing for October 28 stayed near 75–80%.

calls.text: Brent near $112 after the Iran strike-plan report: a confirmed hit on Gulf oil output or a US move toward strikes pushes it above the $112.68 high and lifts the yen and franc; an official denial lets it slip toward $108 by the close
calls.note: Brent did top the high, to about $113, and the yen and franc gained, but without a confirmed hit or an official US move: the report alone and Iran's tanker claims did it.

calls.text: Euro-area consumer confidence 9:00 AM CT (about −17 expected) with France's gap over Germany at its widest since 2011: a weaker reading keeps the euro under $1.12; a steady one lets it recover
calls.note: The reading was weaker (−17.9), yet the euro recovered to about $1.1218 as US yields fell, so the bond rally outweighed the survey.

calls.text: US bond rally on war fears: if the 10-year yield stays near 5.05% into the close, the yen holds its gains near ¥157; if yields rebound on the strong claims figure, the dollar climbs back toward ¥158
calls.note: Yields did not rebound; they fell further, to about 4.95%, on a tech sell-off, and the yen extended its gains to about ¥156.85.

calls.text: US 10-year yield below 5% after the tech sell-off: if Asian and European stocks keep falling overnight, the yen pushes toward ¥156 and the dollar index slips under 101.5; a rebound in stocks lifts yields and the dollar back toward ¥157.5
calls.note: Asian stocks kept falling (Nikkei −1.3%) and the dollar dipped to about ¥156.3, but steadied near ¥156.9 by 12:40 AM CT; the dollar index held at about 101.5 rather than slipping under it.

calls.text: Euro-area flash business surveys Fri 3:00 AM CT (manufacturing ~52.7, services ~52.6 expected), hours before Moody's on France: misses keep the euro near $1.12; beats firm December ECB hike bets and lift it
calls.note: The surveys missed (euro-area composite 51.9, France back in contraction at 48.4), and the euro stayed near $1.12.

calls.text: US flash PMIs Fri 8:45 AM CT (services ~58.0 expected) and Michigan inflation expectations 9:00 AM CT: firm readings lift yields back toward 5% and steady the dollar; soft ones extend the bond rally
calls.note: The surveys were firm on prices and the Michigan inflation outlook ticked up; the 10-year yield rose back to about 5.00% and the dollar index firmed to about 101.8 on Friday.

calls.text: SNB policy summary 2:30 AM CT: worry about a strong franc keeps December cut bets alive and caps the franc; a calmer tone lets it firm
calls.note: Calmer tone: the bank dropped its stronger readiness to intervene and gave no December cut signal. The franc firmed slightly, with the dollar near 0.823, and hit a three-month high against the euro.

calls.text: Saudi departure order: widening across the Gulf or a hit on Saudi output puts Brent well above $110 and lifts the dollar and loonie; staying contained lets oil drift
calls.note: Brent did climb well above $110 (about $113 by the close), but on reports of US–Israeli strike plans and Iranian tanker claims, not a wider departure order. The loonie edged up; the dollar slipped.

calls.text: UK retail sales Fri 1:00 AM CT (−0.2% expected): a strong print lifts December hike bets and the pound; a weak one trims both
calls.note: Sales fell 0.4%, worse than expected, yet the pound reached its strongest against the euro since May 2025 on Friday as a November Bank of England hike stayed near certain.

calls.text: US jobless claims Thu 7:30 AM CT (about 200,000 expected): staying low keeps the Fed's December hike near 90%; a jump trims it and weighs on the dollar
calls.note: Claims stayed low at 194,000 (200,000 expected), near their lowest in decades. December hike bets held near 90% (CME FedWatch, Oct 21); a sharp bond rally later still pulled the dollar lower.

calls.text: Moody's review of France Fri: a downgrade widens France's gap over German yields and weighs on the euro; holding the rating eases the pressure
calls.note: Moody's held France at Aa3; French yields eased on Monday and the euro led the majors in the European morning.

calls.text: Bailey 8:00 AM CT after the 3.5% UK inflation print: backing November without promising more keeps the pound near $1.34; any opening to a December follow-up lifts it; calling energy temporary trims it
calls.note: Neither branch: Bailey gave no new signal on rates. The pound still held near $1.34 (about 1.3395 at the New York close), with December's second hike about a coin toss.

calls.text: US crude oil stocks 9:30 AM CT (industry survey: about −4.9M barrels): a big official draw keeps Brent above $110; a build lets the rebound fade
calls.note: The draw came (−3.1M barrels, far more than forecast) and Brent briefly topped $110.8, but it still faded to $108.82 at the settle after the US Treasury's tanker licence and emergency fuel loans.

calls.text: Pakistan's mediation after Iran's uranium refusal: any confirmed opening drains oil's premium and lifts the euro and yen; more warships and no talks keep Brent near $110 into the close
calls.note: No opening: Rubio called a deal extremely difficult and more US warships headed in. Brent settled at $108.82, near $110 but off its high on Washington's supply moves rather than diplomacy.

calls.text: Japan national CPI Thu 6:30 PM CT (2.1% expected): a hot print keeps the BoJ's December hike near three in four; a soft one fades it and weighs on the yen
calls.note: Neither branch: 2.1% exactly as expected (1.7% prior), though the measure that also leaves out energy jumped to 2.4%. December hike pricing held near 80%.

calls.text: US–Iran framework: confirmation by either government drains oil's risk premium and pulls US long yields lower; another denial puts Brent back toward $110
calls.note: No confirmation from either government, and no fresh denial either. Brent still climbed back toward $110 overnight, on tanker attacks spreading to the Gulf of Oman rather than on the talks.

calls.text: RBA's Hauser 5:30 PM CT: leaning on sticky inflation keeps a November hike near 1 in 3; leaning on the softer job market trims it
calls.note: Hauser leaned on sticky inflation: the outlook is 'materially worse'. Odds of a November hike rose to about 40% from about 30%, and the Aussie hit a three-week high near 0.702.

calls.text: China Q3 GDP 4.5% vs 4.4% fc — the aussie's demand read
calls.note: Beat: 4.5% vs 4.4% fc (q/q 1.2%); retail +1.1% the standout. AUD/USD +0.3-0.5% to ~0.697, the night's best G10 performer; USD/CNH 6.6811, strongest since June 2022. Two-speed beat (factories lead, property -20.6% YTD).

calls.text: Petersburg Oil Terminal drone strike — Baltic supply risk into Monday's open vs the waiver's lower-price pull
calls.note: Fire CONFIRMED (Beglov; Fire Point confirmed its FP-1 hit the terminal); ~1 killed, several injured (figures vary); damage extent still unquantified. Crude's Sunday open came flat — neither the spike nor the tumble; Asia Brent -1.0 to -1.8%.

calls.text: Beirut strike fallout: the haven-bid tell at Monday's open
calls.note: No Hezbollah retaliation as of Monday's open (Qmati: strike crossed a 'red line', leadership to decide; IDF: normal routines). Haven bid stayed sheathed — DXY flat 101.80-101.83, havens ~flat in Asia. The tell held: no escalation, no haven extension.

calls.text: October FOMC priced as a hold (~85%) into the Saturday blackout; December is the live debate
Brent broke $108 on Ukraine refinery strikes — $105-112 range into the weekend (prior $104-108 call broken)
USD/CAD holds 1.41-1.43 into the BoC (Oct 28); Canada CPI Mon the trigger
calls.note: Oct 19: CPI passed without a break — USD/CAD ~1.411 at the NY close, still inside the range. Runs to the Oct 28 decision. Oct 20: dipped to ~1.409, a hair under the floor, as oil and BoC hike bets lifted the loonie. Oct 20 close: broke below the floor — USD/CAD ~1.406, strongest loonie since Sep 22, on BoC hike pricing (~80–85%) and Alberta's vote to remain.
The tripwire never bit — Friday's waiver suspends the duties outright with no end date. Superseded by the ~Dec 17 60-day review clock.
calls.text: Graham Act Oct-18 tripwire: waivers extended or enforcement begins — oil's Sunday open is the tell
Iran deal Sunday signing: Trump's 'OPEN TO ALL' vs Tehran's 'not tomorrow' — the strait itself is the verdict
calls.note: No signed deal carried by any major wire by 4pm CT Sunday; Trump's 'complete' claim stands unverified against Tehran's 'talks stalled'. Aggregator 'markets celebrate' content held — its futures numbers contradict Friday's verified settles. The signing test is claim day, not done day.

calls.text: Canada CPI Mon 7:30am CT (TD 3.2%, UBS 3.3%, RBC 3.0%): hot (3.3%+) revives the Oct 28 hike; soft (3.0%-) buries it to December
calls.note: Neither branch: 3.1% vs 3.2% expected, core measures cooled to 1.8–1.9%. October stayed about 1 in 4 (a hold), with about one quarter-point hike priced by December; consumers' inflation expectations rose to ~3.9% in the BoC survey. Correction (Oct 20): by Monday's close swaps had jumped to ~87% for an October hike on Macklem's Saturday forecast warning; the 1-in-4 figure was stale.

calls.text: UK CPI Wed 1am CT (3.4% fc vs 3.1%): 3.5%+ starts pricing a December follow-up; soft reopens Bailey's 2027 read
calls.note: Hot branch: 3.5% vs 3.4% expected (3.1% in August), the highest in 11 months. November's hike is near certain; how much December moved was not yet verified at write.

calls.text: NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (ANZ 3.8% y/y): hot settles the RBNZ's two-way bet toward the hike side
calls.note: Not hot: inflation came in at 3.7%, a touch soft. The hike side still settled anyway, with October 28 now about 98% priced.

calls.text: Japan CPI Fri + BoJ Oct 29-30: Ueda's 'quite close' language tested — October hike stays ~25%
calls.note: Oct 19: swaps now put an October 30 hike under 5% (BBH), below the ~25% in the call. December ~80% unchanged. October hike odds fell to about 4%, far below the ~25% in the call; Japan's inflation came in at 2.1% as expected and December (~80%) is now the meeting that matters.

calls.text: France's revenue-section budget vote Tue: a clean pass narrows the French–German spread (~141bp); a defeat or big concessions widens it and weighs on the euro
calls.note: No vote on Tuesday: it was pushed to October 27, so neither branch played out.

calls.text: UK jobs Tue 1 AM CT (earnings ~3.8% expected): sticky pay firms the BoE hike case before Wednesday's inflation; cooling pay backs Bailey's calmer view
calls.note: Sticky side won: unemployment fell to 4.7% (4.9% expected) and regular pay rose 3.7% (3.6% expected); total pay and claims were softer. Pound +0.3% to ~1.334.

calls.text: Konarak follow-through: a US confirmation or more strikes keeps oil's supply premium and lifts US yields; silence lets the morning's waiver drop resume
calls.note: No confirmation (a US official denied the strike) and no new strike overnight, yet the premium held: Brent ~$109.8 Tuesday on low Gulf flows and Iran's Hormuz claims. The waiver-driven drop did not resume.

calls.text: BoC Oct 28 with ~87% priced for a hike: a hike is mostly in the loonie already; a hold would be the surprise and hit it
calls.note: The Bank of Canada hiked as priced, and the loonie barely moved on the day.

calls.text: NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (~3.8% y/y): near forecast keeps the ~80% hike pricing; clearly soft reopens the hold and weighs on the kiwi
calls.note: Near forecast (3.7% vs 3.8%) and hike pricing held, rising to about 98%; the kiwi dipped only briefly.
